Photonic chip race between United States, Russia, China and Netherlands 

Photonic chips (also called optical or light-based chips) use photons (light) instead of electrons for computation, data movement, or interconnects. 

They promise major advantages over traditional silicon electronic chips: much higher bandwidth, lower energy consumption (critical for power-hungry AI data centers), less heat generation, and potential for faster processing in specific tasks like matrix multiplications or AI inference. 

List of nations that have started production (including pilot, test, or commercial-scale lines) of photonic chips (photonic integrated circuits or PICs) as of early 2026:

United States — Long-standing leader in silicon photonics production. Companies like GlobalFoundries (New York) manufacture silicon photonics platforms (e.g., GF Fotonix) at scale for interconnects, AI, and quantum applications (used by PsiQuantum, Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, etc.). 

Other foundries such as Tower Semiconductor (with fabs in the US, Israel, and Japan) and Intel also produce silicon photonics. US-based QCi operates a thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) fab in Arizona. 

China — Launched its first dedicated pilot production line in June 2025 at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's CHIPX (Wuxi) for thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonic chips on 6-inch wafers (capacity: ~12,000 wafers/year). 

Additional silicon photonics pilot lines exist (e.g., in Northwest China/Shaanxi, 8-inch platform in 2025). China also has photonic quantum chip production efforts (e.g., Shenzhen factory).

Netherlands — Strong European leader. SMART Photonics has been producing indium phosphide (InP) photonic wafers for years. 

A major new indium phosphide photonic chip pilot line (part of EU's PIXEurope) began construction in Eindhoven in 2025/early 2026 and was officially launched as a European pilot facility in March 2026. It aims for industrial-scale 6-inch wafer production.

Russia — Started its first dedicated photonic integrated circuit production line in Moscow (Zelenograd) in late 2025. This includes test/pilot production with capacity for up to 2,000 wafers and hundreds of thousands of PICs annually.
